background: In February 2026, the automotive marketplace CarGurus was the target of a data breach attributed to the threat actor ShinyHunters . Following an attempted extortion, the data was published publicly and contained more than 12M email addresses across multiple files including user account ID mappings, finance pre-qualification application data and dealer account and subscription information. Impacted data also included names, phone numbers, physical and IP addresses, and auto finance application outcomes.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
motive: In February 2026, the automotive marketplace CarGurus was the target of a data breach attributed to the threat actor ShinyHunters .

Following an attempted extortion, the data was published publicly and contained more than 12M email addresses across multiple files including user account ID mappings, finance pre-qualification application data and dealer account and subscription information.
outcome: 12,461,887 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, IP addresses, Names, Phone numbers, Physical addresses.
editorial: One phrase in the field list deserves a stop: finance pre-qualification application data. Those are people who asked a car marketplace what they could borrow, a question nobody asks idly, and the answer is sitting beside their name, phone number and home address. Intent is the part of a breach that rarely makes the summary and reliably makes the fraud.

Knowing that someone is shopping for a car, and roughly what they can finance, tells a caller which pretext will land: a rate they have been approved for, a deposit to hold a vehicle, a dealer following up on the application they really did fill in last week. Generic scams get hung up on. This one continues a conversation the victim started.

Dealer account and subscription records were in the same release, which hands the same caller both ends of that conversation, the buyer's details and a real dealership to impersonate. The defence is procedural rather than technical: anything about a vehicle purchase, a finance offer or a deposit gets confirmed by ringing the dealer on a number you looked up yourself.
Never the number in the message, however well the message knows you.

fields.name: Physical addresses
fields.why: Where someone actually lives. Combined with a name this moves the risk off the internet.

fields.name: Phone numbers
fields.why: Enables SIM-swap attacks against SMS two-factor codes, and puts the number on scam-call lists indefinitely.

fields.name: IP addresses
fields.why: Approximate location at the time of use, and a way to correlate accounts across services.

fields.name: Names
fields.why: Turns an anonymous address into an identified person, which is what makes targeted phishing possible.

fields.name: Email addresses
fields.why: The address becomes a confirmed, active target, expect more phishing, better aimed.

actions: Move two-factor authentication off SMS and onto an authenticator app, which a SIM swap cannot intercept.
Be sceptical of post and callers who already know your address, knowing it is no longer evidence of anything.
Expect better-aimed phishing. A message that already knows your name and where you have an account is the whole point of a breach like this.
breach.scale_line: That is about 46% of the population of Australia.
